title: The practice of Medina
hook: Malik gave weight to the living practice of Medina's people

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Muwatta, and your line: the well-trodden path. Where did you do one small good thing on a route you walk every day? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

In the Muwatta's chapter on trade, Malik records a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: a buyer and a seller each keep the right to call off the deal as long as they haven't parted. Then, right under it, Malik adds a note. Among us, he says, there's no fixed limit for this, and no practice of acting on it. He has just written the hadith down himself, carefully, with its chain. And in the same breath he says Medina doesn't do it that way. That isn't carelessness. It's a method, and it's the heart of his school. Today: the practice of Medina.
screen: `A HADITH ON CALLING OFF A SALE.` → `MALIK'S NOTE: NOT DONE HERE.` → `NOT CARELESS: A METHOD.`

segments.voice: The phrase in Arabic is 'amal ahl al-Madinah, the practice of the people of Medina. Start with Malik's reasoning. Medina was where the Prophet lived his last years, where the companions prayed behind him and traded in his market. Their children watched them, and their grandchildren watched their children. So what Medina did, day after day, was itself a kind of report. Not one person remembering one sentence, but a whole city carrying a way of life from parent to child. Next, how much weight he gave it. For Malik, where the settled practice of Medina went one way and a single narrator's report went another, the practice could carry more weight. The report might be true, but limited, or later set aside, and the city's daily life would know. That's what the note under the trade hadith is doing. Then, a friendly argument. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd, a great scholar of Egypt, wrote Malik a letter of real respect and real disagreement. The companions, he said, didn't all stay in Medina. They went to Egypt, Syria and Iraq, and taught there too. Medina's practice is precious, but it isn't the only living practice. Malik's school kept its method; the letter was preserved, and readers still point to it as scholars disagreeing well. Last, the point under it all. Some knowledge lives on paper. Some lives in how people stand, greet, trade and pray. Malik took the second kind seriously enough to build a school on it.
screen: `'AMAL AHL AL-MADINAH.` · `A WHOLE CITY AS A REPORT.` · `AL-LAYTH: THE COMPANIONS WENT ELSEWHERE TOO.` · `KNOWLEDGE THAT LIVES IN PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn from a community's practice. Bring to mind a group whose ways you learned by watching, not reading. A family at holidays. A kitchen at a restaurant job. A mosque, a team, a choir. What did you learn there that nobody ever wrote down? How to set the table. When to stay quiet. Who gets served first. Pick one of those things and hold it. Notice that you carry it now, the way Medina carried its practice. If you pray, you can remember the people who taught you without meaning to. The bell holds the time.
The practice of Medina. 'Amal ahl al-Madinah: the settled way the people of Medina lived, which Malik treated as a living report of the Prophet's way. Today's word.
Your line: the living practice. Today, watch one thing a community around you does without explaining it, and ask someone where it came from. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Maliki jurists treat the settled practice of the people of Medina as strong evidence of the Prophet's sunnah, at times preferring it over a report carried by a single narrator.

fork.setup: you're Malik. a sound-looking hadith says buyer and seller may call off a deal until they part, but Medina doesn't practice it. what do you write?
options: leave the hadith out of your book.
record the hadith, and note that Medina's practice differs.
change Medina's practice to match the hadith.
fork.reveal: he records it, with its chain, and adds: among us there's no fixed limit for this and no practice of acting on it.

original.note: Arabic: the practice of the people of Medina; 'amal means action, what is done.

trapdoor: what you thought: Islamic law is built only from written reports.
what it means: for Malik, what a whole city did every day was itself evidence.
what a scholar hears: 'amal ahl al-Madinah weighed against khabar al-wahid, and al-Layth ibn Sa'd's letter to Malik.

sources.ref: Muwatta Malik, Kitab al-Buyu' (the option of buyer and seller until they part, with Malik's comment)
Letter of al-Layth ibn Sa'd to Malik (preserved in Ibn Qayyim, I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in)

notes: The khiyar al-majlis hadith (Ibn Umar) in the Muwatta and Malik's comment that there is no fixed limit or practice of acting on it in Medina: confirm the placement and paraphrase.

'Where the settled practice of Medina went one way and a single narrator's report another, the practice could carry more weight': confirm framing of the Maliki position (and the distinction between transmitted practice and practice by ijtihad, left out here).
Al-Layth ibn Sa'd's letter (companions in Egypt, Syria, Iraq): confirm content and where it is preserved.
'The Prophet lived his last years' in Medina: stated generally, no number given.
Original: عمل أهل المدينة; confirm pronunciation.
Editor pass: softened 'the letter is still read, and it's a model' into an attributed claim.
